newsitem.title: THAILAND: Thai election will boost economy, stocks - analysts.
newsitem.headline: Thai election will boost economy, stocks - analysts.

text.p: Prime Minister Banharn Silpa-archa's surprise in breaking a deadlock over his successor by calling snap elections was welcomed by analysts on Friday as a boost for the economy and the battered Thai stock market.

They applauded Banharn's move to block his rival, Defence Minister Chavalit Yongchaiyudh, from securing the premiership, saying it raised hopes the country could get a more qualified economic team seen needed to shore up the slowing economy.

"Excellent. This is just the best scenario I had in mind. (Banharn's) decision offers the best chance for substantial government changes, for an alternative to Chavalit," said Sriyan Pietersz, chief strategist of Bangkok Nomura.

Chavalit had earlier been tipped as the frontrunner to replace Banharn after the unpopular prime minister was forced by coalition allies to resign in exchange for their support to help him win a no-confidence vote in parliament.

Pietersz said he expected Thailand's weak bourse, which declined to a near three-year low this month, to stage a sharp recovery from Monday, to be followed by consolidation in the run-up to the election scheduled for November 17.

Barry Yates, research director of Multi-Credit Corp of Thailand, said the market's composite SET Index could surge at least 100 points during the next few weeks before encountering profit taking at the 1,150-1,200 level. The index closed Friday at 1,047.95.

During the no-confidence debate last week, Banharn was attacked by opposition politicians for mismanagement that they said was responsible for Thailand's flagging economic growth this year, projected to be the slowest in a decade.
Private economists predict the Thai Gross Domestic Product would expand about seven percent in 1996 against the central bank target of 7.8 percent and the 8.6 percent growth in 1995.
Thai exports rose only 2.9 percent during January/July against a 26.5 percent increase a year ago.
Somchai Phagaphasvivat, a political scientist of Thammasat University, hailed Banharn's decision as a victory for the Thai democractic process.

"The decision makes it more flexible for Thai politics to work out compromises for conflicting interests. The parliament dissolution gives people new hopes and boosts their faith in politics," he said.
Pietersz of Bangkok Nomura agreed with most analysts that the Democrat Party, led by former Prime Minister Chuan Leekpai, could emerge the biggest winner in the next election.
He said Chuan's Democrat Party may team up with the Palang Dharma Party of business tycoon Thaksin Shinawatra and other opposition parties to form a new government after the election.
Palang Dharma has its stronghold in Bangkok, where urban voters and its business community have been highly critical of the Banharn government in the past 14 months.
Pietersz said he was pleased that the election would be held in 45-50 days instead of Thailand's usual practice of allowing a 90-day election campaign period.

Analysts earlier feared that political uncertainty arising from the impasse over Banharn's successor or a long run-up to an election would leave an administrative vacuum that could disrupt government efforts to revive the economy.
